content.p: On a windswept headland at the western tip of the Dingle peninsula, in November 1580, a garrison of Italian, Spanish and Irish men held out for about three days against an English army and the guns of English ships. They then gave up the fort. Within a day, on the orders of the Lord Deputy of Ireland, Arthur Grey, Baron Grey de Wilton, most of them were put to death. Grey himself reported the toll to Queen Elizabeth I in a single plain sentence: "There were 600 slayne."

The fort, Dún an Óir, stood above Smerwick harbour in County Kerry. Historians continue to disagree about whether Grey had offered the defenders their lives, and about how many of the dead were fighting men. Nobody disputes that the killing happened. It became one of the best-known atrocities of the Elizabethan conquest of Ireland, and the argument over it has lasted more than four centuries.
content.h2: A rebellion with a papal army
content.p: The Second Desmond Rebellion, which began in 1579, was fought mainly in Munster. Heritage Ireland, the Office of Public Works site page, describes several strands in it: an effort to win a measure of Irish independence from England, part of a wider Spanish and English struggle for dominance, a clash between Gaelic and Gaelicised Old English families such as the Desmonds and Fitzgeralds and new English colonisers, and a Catholic crusade against the Protestant queen. The Irish Times writer, visiting the site in 2022, added the English crown's wish to take the lands of Munster's lords and hand them to English planters.

Voices from the Dawn, a heritage project, says the force that sailed into Smerwick on 10 September 1580 was led by an Italian captain, Sebastiano di San Giuseppe, and was recruited with money supplied by Pope Gregory XIII. It gives the strength as 600 Italian, Spanish and Basque troops. Other accounts give smaller figures: the Irish Catholic cites 400 to 500 soldiers, and the Times, in a 2004 report, speaks of about 600 men. Visitors to the site today are told by the West Kerry museum that the garrison was 700 to 800 strong.

The newcomers began fortifying the old promontory fort. According to Heritage Ireland, they started building newer, more modern defences, but had not finished when Grey arrived. The Irish rebels they had hoped to join were slow to come. Voices from the Dawn says only 17 Irishmen joined them.
content.h2: The deputy who came to Kerry
content.p: Grey landed at Dublin on 12 August 1580 to take over from Sir William Pelham. Within two weeks he marched into the Wicklow hills against the rebels of the Pale. The Irish Biography entry says he entered the defile of Glenmalure on 25 August against the advice of men who knew Irish warfare, and that his army was ambushed and defeated there. Voices from the Dawn says he lost 800 men. The Irish Times says the beating he took in Wicklow from its rebel leader weighed on him afterwards, and suggests it left him little inclined to be generous.

Word of the landing at Smerwick then drew him south. The Irish Biography entry says he took a small force of about 1,000 and invested the fort on 31 October. Grey's own despatch, written from the camp on 12 November, dates his camp before the fort to 7 November, and says storms and a late-arriving fleet had held him up for days. Heritage Ireland and the Times also put the attack on 7 November The sources give no reason for the gap.

His own army was small. Grey told the Queen that she had "but 800" men at the service, and Heritage Ireland and the Times use the same figure. The Irish Times and Voices from the Dawn say the English army numbered about 4,000, and the sources do not reconcile the two. The ships were commanded by Admiral Sir William Winter, with Captain Richard Bingham's vessel in the bay. Grey wrote that the fleet's arrival, after days of storms, made the attack possible, because he had no way to haul heavy guns overland.

Grey's despatch gives an unusually detailed account of the days that followed. He rode out with Bingham to view the ground, and a short skirmish with the garrison's musketeers left three of their men dead and none of his. The English landed their artillery the same afternoon and dug a trench closer to the fort overnight. The next morning, he wrote, two culverins opened on the fort and the garrison answered with muskets for an hour or two, until two of their best guns were put out of action. In the following night the defenders made four sorties to drive off the diggers. An officer, John Cheeke, was hit in the head while looking over the trench; Grey wrote that he lived on for a time and made a pious confession of faith, and spent a long digression on him.

The fort had no way out. Mount Brandon rose behind the English army, and the ship's guns lay off the headland. Voices from the Dawn adds that after three days of what it calls a one-sided battle the defenders hoisted a sheet and called for a parley. Grey's own account matches that: he wrote that a man leapt to the top of the rampart with a sheet as an ensign and asked for terms.

Grey's despatch says he spoke first with the garrison's camp master, then with a Spanish captain he insisted on seeing. The Spaniard told him that the Spanish king had not sent them and that they had been gathered on the orders of a governor at Bilbo. Another man said the Pope had sent them. Grey told them that no terms were available: they must hand over the fort and "yield their selves to my will for life or death". He wrote that the colonel, after pleading for a night's delay, which Grey refused, put himself at Grey's mercy and gave hostages. In the morning the colonel came out with ten or twelve of his officers, "trayling theyr ensignes rolled vp", and presented them.

What followed Grey set down in a few lines. He sent gentlemen in to see the weapons laid down and to guard the stores. Then, in his words, "putt I in certeyn bandes, who streight fell to execution. There were 600 slayne". He added that the men he spared were given to his captains and gentlemen, and that 400 of the 600 were as "gallant and goodly personages" as he had ever seen. The colonel's chest of money, which Grey said totalled 329 pounds in plate, was shared among his soldiers.

Whether the garrison had been promised their lives is where accounts diverge. Voices from the Dawn says one side holds that Grey accepted an unconditional surrender, as his own letter states, while another cites "high authority" that the defenders were promised their lives. The Tudor Society says Grey massacred them "even though he'd promised them their lives". The Irish Times writer says only that there is no doubt about what happened after they gave up, whether or not mercy had been offered. Voices from the Dawn also reports an account that the colonel tried to bargain for a share of the treasure by handing over some of his Irish allies.

The date of the killing is also given two ways. History Today, the Cambridge journal article and the West Kerry museum place it on 10 November. Voices from the Dawn and the Irish Biography entry say the garrison surrendered on the 10th and was killed the next morning, 11 November. Grey's despatch is dated the 12th.

Grey's figure of 600 is the one the later sources repeat. The Irish Times writer states that the dead included pregnant women and children, as well as Italians, Spaniards and Irishmen. Heritage Ireland also says women and children were among those killed. The Irish Biography entry says a few women and a priest were hanged, that officers were reserved for ransom, and that the bodies were stripped and laid out on the sand.

Local tradition, which Voices from the Dawn and the Irish Times set down, holds that the prisoners were beheaded in a field now called Gort a Ghearradh, the Field of the Cutting; that their bodies were thrown into the sea; and that the heads were buried in a neighbouring field, Gort na gCeann, the Field of the Heads. Voices from the Dawn says only 13 men, thought likely to be ransomed, were spared. The Sunday Times, reporting in 2004, said historians find the evidence confusing and that Grey made no mention of decapitation.

The same sources report that a smaller group suffered separately. The Irish Catholic says that officers who had been spared were offered life if they renounced their faith and that, when they refused, an ironsmith broke their arms and legs and they were hanged after a day and a night, though the Irish Catholic words it as "reportedly". Voices from the Dawn describes a priest and two other men treated in the same way, and says marksmen later used the bodies for target practice.
content.h2: Spenser, Raleigh and a letter in an elegant hand
content.p: Two famous names are attached to the story. Edmund Spenser, later the author of The Faerie Queene, was Grey's secretary. A scholar writing in PMLA identified a letter that he called virtually conclusive proof of Spenser's presence at Smerwick, and judged it probable that Spenser himself wrote out Grey's despatch to the Queen, in his careful Italian hand. Voices from the Dawn suggests that some wording credited to Grey probably came from Spenser, and says that Spenser later defended Grey's methods in his prose work on Ireland, A View of the Present State of Ireland, written in 1596 and published after his death.

The second name is Walter Raleigh. The Irish Biography entry says he was one of the officers commanding the party that carried out the Deputy's orders. Library Ireland's nineteenth-century guide says the killing was later brought against Raleigh as one of the charges at his trial, and that he defended himself by pleading that he was a subordinate who had to obey his superior. Local tradition goes further: the Sunday Times reported that Dingle children were warned to "watch out" for Raleigh if they misbehaved.
content.h2: Grey's recall and the argument over law
content.p: The Irish Biography entry says the war in Munster was virtually over by the summer of 1582 and that Grey left Ireland in August of that year. It gives two explanations for his recall, without choosing between them. The historian Froude, it says, held that Grey had asked to go; the older writer Cox claimed the rebels had contrived to have him painted him at court as a bloody man, and that, as he put it, "there was little left for the Queen to reign over but carcasses and ashes". Voices from the Dawn says some accounts blame the massacre for his recall, and also cites a modern historian who thinks his poor financial management ended his term. Grey later sat on the commission at the trial of Mary, Queen of Scots, and died in 1593.

Voices from the Dawn says the phrase "Grey's Faith" came to mean deceitful or treacherous. Library Ireland's history says the phrase became known even on the Continent. A 2019 article in the Journal of British Studies argues that Grey justified the killings to the Queen and to the English public by treating the papal troops as brigands and pirates, "a common enemy to all", who had no standing as lawful enemies under the law of nations. It sets this against the view of Vincent Carey, who stressed Grey's anti-Catholic reasoning. The University of York notes that accounts of the event survive in Italian, Latin, English and Gaelic and that the commonly used version comes largely from Grey and Spenser.

The Irish poet Seamus Heaney evoked the event in his poem "Ocean's Love to Ireland" with the lines about "Smerwick sowed with the mouthing corpses of six hundred papists". In 1980 a memorial by the sculptor Cliodhna Cussen was put up on the site, in Gort na gCeann; the Irish Times writer describes twelve carved heads on its face.

Little of the fort remains. Voices from the Dawn says that metal-detector hunters found four fragments of a bronze gun beneath the cliffs in 1969. The earthworks that survive are what remains of the Spanish bastions that were never finished, according to Heritage Ireland, and the West Kerry museum calls the site the most intact siege site in Ireland. The Sunday Times in 2004 reported local residents' claims of skeletons appearing on a nearby beach and their petition for an archaeological "ranger". Voices from the Dawn treated such stories as folklore.
